prompt: In what form do amino acids mainly exist in aqueous solution at a physiological pH of 7.3?

choices.text: As a dipolar ion (zwitterion), with a –CO2^− group and an –NH3^+ group
As an uncharged molecule, with a –CO2H group and an –NH2 group
choices.why: At pH 7.3 the carboxyl group is deprotonated and the amino group is protonated, so both groups are charged.

choices.text: As a cation, with a –CO2H group and an –NH3^+ group
choices.why: This cation forms in aqueous acid, when the zwitterion accepts a proton onto its –CO2^− group.

choices.text: As an anion, with a –CO2^− group and an –NH2 group
choices.why: This anion forms in aqueous base, when the zwitterion loses a proton from its –NH3^+ group.

explanation: At pH 7.3 a carboxyl group exists as the carboxylate anion and an amino group as the ammonium cation. Amino acids therefore exist in water mainly as a dipolar ion, or zwitterion (from the German zwitter, meaning “hybrid”).

prompt: Amino acid zwitterions are internal salts. Which set of physical properties do amino acids have as a result?

choices.text: Large dipole moments, relatively soluble in water, insoluble in hydrocarbons, crystalline with relatively high melting points
Small dipole moments, insoluble in water, soluble in hydrocarbons, crystalline with relatively high melting points
choices.why: Salts are very polar: amino acids have large dipole moments and dissolve in water rather than in hydrocarbons.

choices.text: Large dipole moments, relatively soluble in water, insoluble in hydrocarbons, liquids with low melting points
choices.why: Like other salts, amino acids are crystalline with relatively high melting points.

choices.text: Small dipole moments, soluble in hydrocarbons, insoluble in water, liquids with low melting points
choices.why: This describes a nonpolar molecular compound, the opposite of a salt-like zwitterion.

explanation: Because zwitterions are internal salts, amino acids have many of the properties of salts: large dipole moments, relative solubility in water but insolubility in hydrocarbons, and crystallinity with relatively high melting points.

prompt: Amino acids are described as amphiprotic. What does that mean?

choices.text: They can react either as acids or as bases, depending on the circumstances
They contain both a chirality center and a plane of symmetry
choices.why: Amphiprotic is about acid–base behavior, not stereochemistry.

choices.text: They are soluble in both water and hydrocarbons
choices.why: Amino acids are soluble in water but insoluble in hydrocarbons; amphiprotic refers to acid–base behavior.

choices.text: They can act only as acids, because both groups can lose a proton
choices.why: The zwitterion can also act as a base: its –CO2^− group accepts a proton in acid solution.

explanation: Amino acids are amphiprotic: they can react either as acids or as bases. In aqueous acid the zwitterion acts as a base, and in aqueous base it acts as an acid.

prompt: What happens to an amino acid zwitterion in aqueous acid solution?

choices.text: It acts as a base, accepting a proton onto its –CO2^− group to give a cation
It acts as an acid, losing a proton from its –NH3^+ group to give an anion
choices.why: That happens in aqueous base, not in acid.

choices.text: It acts as a base, accepting a proton onto its –NH3^+ group to give a dication
choices.why: The –NH3^+ group is already protonated; the proton goes onto the –CO2^− group.

choices.text: It acts as an acid, losing a proton from its –CO2^− group
choices.why: A carboxylate group has no acidic proton to lose; in acid it gains a proton instead.

explanation: In aqueous acid solution, an amino acid zwitterion is a base that accepts a proton onto its –CO2^− group to yield a cation. In aqueous base, it is an acid that loses a proton from its –NH3^+ group to form an anion.

prompt: All 20 common amino acids in proteins are α-amino acids. What does that mean?

choices.text: The amino group is on the α carbon, the carbon next to the carbonyl group
The amino group is attached directly to the carbonyl carbon
choices.why: That would be an amide; in an α-amino acid the amino group is on the carbon next to the carbonyl group.

choices.text: The amino group is on the last carbon of the side chain
choices.why: The amino group of an α-amino acid is on the α carbon; the side chain is the substituent attached to that carbon.

choices.text: The amino acid has the α (L) configuration at its chirality center
choices.why: α describes the position of the amino group, not the configuration; L refers to configuration.

explanation: All 20 common amino acids are α-amino acids: the amino group is a substituent on the α carbon, the one next to the carbonyl group. They differ in their side chain, the substituent attached to the α carbon.

prompt: How many of the 20 common amino acids are primary amines, RNH2?
explanation: Nineteen of the twenty amino acids are primary amines, RNH2, differing only in their side chains. The exception is proline, a secondary amine whose nitrogen and α carbon are part of a five-membered pyrrolidine ring.

prompt: Which of the 20 common amino acids is a secondary amine?

choices.why: Lysine's α-amino group is primary; its extra amino group is in the side chain, not a ring nitrogen.
Histidine's α-amino group is primary; the imidazole nitrogens are in its side chain.
Glycine, H2NCH2CO2H, is a primary amine with no side chain other than H.

explanation: Nineteen of the 20 amino acids are primary amines. Proline is a secondary amine: its nitrogen and α carbon atoms are part of a ring.

prompt: What ring contains the nitrogen and α carbon of proline?

choices.why: Proline's ring is five-membered: a pyrrolidine.
The imidazole ring is in histidine's side chain, and it doesn't include the α carbon.
Proline's ring is saturated; it is a pyrrolidine, not an aromatic pyrrole.

explanation: Proline is a secondary amine whose nitrogen and α carbon atoms are part of a five-membered pyrrolidine ring.

prompt: What are the three- and one-letter abbreviations for glutamine?

choices.why: Glu and E are the abbreviations for glutamic acid.
Gly and G are the abbreviations for glycine.
G is the one-letter code for glycine; glutamine is Q.

explanation: According to Table 26.1.1, glutamine is Gln (Q). Be careful with the look-alikes: glutamic acid is Glu (E) and glycine is Gly (G).

prompt: Which amino acid has the one-letter abbreviation W?

choices.why: Tyrosine is Y (Tyr).
Threonine is T (Thr).
Valine is V (Val).

explanation: Table 26.1.1 lists tryptophan as Trp, W. The other “T” amino acids are tyrosine (Tyr, Y) and threonine (Thr, T).

prompt: Which amino acid has the one-letter abbreviation K?

choices.why: Arginine is R (Arg).
Leucine is L (Leu).
Asparagine is N (Asn).

explanation: Table 26.1.1 lists lysine as Lys, K. Lysine is one of the three basic amino acids, along with arginine (Arg, R) and histidine (His, H).

prompt: Which amino acid has the one-letter abbreviation D?

choices.why: Asparagine is N (Asn).
Glutamic acid is E (Glu).
Glutamine is Q (Gln).

explanation: Table 26.1.1 lists aspartic acid as Asp, D. Its look-alikes are asparagine (Asn, N), glutamic acid (Glu, E), and glutamine (Gln, Q).

prompt: How many of the 20 common amino acids are classified as having neutral side chains?
explanation: The 20 common amino acids are classified by their side chains: 15 are neutral, 2 (aspartic acid and glutamic acid) are acidic, and 3 (lysine, arginine, and histidine) are basic.

prompt: Which three amino acids have basic amino groups in their side chains?

choices.why: Asparagine's side chain is an amide, and it is classified as neutral.
Glutamine and tryptophan are classified as neutral amino acids in Table 26.1.1.

choices.text: Aspartic acid, glutamic acid, and histidine
choices.why: Aspartic acid and glutamic acid have acidic side chains, not basic ones.

explanation: Three amino acids, lysine, arginine, and histidine, have basic amino groups in their side chains. Aspartic acid and glutamic acid have an extra carboxylic acid group, and the other 15 are neutral.

prompt: Which two amino acids have an extra carboxylic acid group in their side chains?

choices.why: Asparagine and glutamine have amide side chains and are classified as neutral.
Cysteine (a thiol) and tyrosine (a phenol) have weakly acidic side chains but are usually classified as neutral.
Serine and threonine have alcohol side chains and are neutral.

explanation: Two amino acids, aspartic acid and glutamic acid, are classified as acidic because they have an extra carboxylic acid function in their side chains.

prompt: Which two amino acids are usually classified as neutral but have weakly acidic side chains that can be deprotonated in a sufficiently basic solution?

choices.why: These are classified as acidic amino acids, not neutral ones.
Their side chains are amides; the book names cysteine and tyrosine as the weakly acidic neutral ones.
These have basic side chains and are classified as basic amino acids.

explanation: Cysteine (a thiol) and tyrosine (a phenol), although usually classified as neutral amino acids, have weakly acidic side chains that can be deprotonated in a sufficiently basic solution. Table 26.1.1 gives side-chain pK_a values of 8.18 for cysteine and 10.07 for tyrosine.

prompt: Which basic amino acid has a side chain that is not quite basic enough to be protonated at pH 7.3?

choices.why: At pH 7.3 the basic side-chain nitrogen of lysine is protonated.
At pH 7.3 the basic side-chain nitrogens of arginine are protonated.
Glutamic acid is acidic; at pH 7.3 its side-chain carboxyl is deprotonated.

explanation: At pH 7.3, the side-chain carboxyl groups of aspartic acid and glutamic acid are deprotonated and the basic side-chain nitrogens of lysine and arginine are protonated. Histidine, which has an imidazole ring in its side chain, is not quite basic enough to be protonated at pH 7.3.

prompt: Why is the pyrrole-like, singly bonded nitrogen in histidine's imidazole ring nonbasic?

choices.text: Its lone pair of electrons is part of the six-π-electron aromatic imidazole ring
It has no lone pair of electrons
choices.why: It has a lone pair, but that pair is tied up in the aromatic ring.

choices.text: Its lone pair is delocalized onto a neighboring carbonyl group
choices.why: That explains why amide nitrogens are nonbasic; histidine's ring nitrogen has no carbonyl neighbor.

choices.text: It is already protonated at all pH values
choices.why: The book's reason is that its lone pair belongs to the aromatic sextet.

explanation: Only the pyridine-like, doubly bonded nitrogen in histidine is basic. The pyrrole-like singly bonded nitrogen is nonbasic because its lone pair of electrons is part of the six-π-electron aromatic imidazole ring.

prompt: Which nonprotein amino acid is found in blood and is linked to coronary heart disease?

choices.why: GABA is found in the brain, where it acts as a neurotransmitter.
Thyroxine is found in the thyroid gland, where it acts as a hormone.
Selenocysteine is not a nonprotein amino acid; it is one of two extra amino acids found in proteins of some organisms.

explanation: More than 700 nonprotein amino acids are found in nature. γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) is a neurotransmitter in the brain, homocysteine is found in blood and is linked to coronary heart disease, and thyroxine is a hormone in the thyroid gland.

prompt: How does the book describe selenocysteine and pyrrolysine?

choices.text: As amino acids found in proteins of some organisms, beyond the 20 common ones
As nonprotein amino acids that act as hormones in the thyroid gland
choices.why: Thyroxine is the hormone example; selenocysteine and pyrrolysine are found in some organisms in addition to the 20 common protein amino acids.

choices.text: As two of the 20 common amino acids that are found in all proteins
choices.why: They are not among the 20 in Table 26.1.1; they are extras found in some organisms.

choices.text: As the D enantiomers of cysteine and lysine, made only in the laboratory
choices.why: They are separate amino acids, not enantiomers of common ones.

explanation: In addition to the 20 amino acids commonly found in proteins, 2 others, selenocysteine and pyrrolysine, are found in some organisms, and more than 700 nonprotein amino acids are also found in nature.

prompt: Which common amino acid has no chirality center at its α carbon?

choices.why: Alanine's α carbon carries H, CH3, –NH3^+, and –CO2^−, four different groups, so it is a chirality center.
Proline's α carbon is part of a ring and still bears four different groups.
Cysteine's α carbon is a chirality center; it is the L amino acid with the R configuration.

explanation: Except for glycine, H2NCH2CO2H, the α carbons of amino acids are chirality centers. Glycine's α carbon carries two hydrogens, so it is not a chirality center.

prompt: A naturally occurring amino acid is drawn in a Fischer projection with the –CO2^− group at the top and the side chain pointing down. Where is the –NH3^+ group?

choices.why: With –CO2^− at the top and the side chain down, an –NH3^+ group on the right shows the nonnatural D amino acid.

choices.text: At the bottom, replacing the side chain
choices.why: The side chain points down; the –NH3^+ group goes on one of the horizontal positions.

choices.text: At the top, replacing the –CO2^− group
choices.why: The –CO2^− group is placed at the top; the –NH3^+ group is horizontal.

explanation: Naturally occurring amino acids are drawn in Fischer projections with the –CO2^− group at the top, the side chain pointing down, and the –NH3^+ group on the left. Because of their stereochemical similarity to L sugars, they are called L amino acids; the nonnatural enantiomers are D amino acids.

prompt: Of the 19 L amino acids that have a chirality center at the α carbon, how many have the S configuration there?
explanation: Glycine has no chirality center, leaving 19 L amino acids. Eighteen of them have the S configuration at the α carbon; cysteine is the only one with an R configuration (Exercise 26.1.2).

prompt: Cysteine is the only L amino acid with an R configuration at the α carbon. Why?

choices.text: Sulfur in its –CH2SH side chain makes that group outrank –CO2H
Cysteine's –NH3^+ group is on the right in its Fischer projection
choices.why: All L amino acids, including cysteine, have –NH3^+ on the left; the R label comes from a change in group ranking.

choices.text: Cysteine in proteins is a D amino acid, unlike the others
choices.why: Cysteine in proteins is an L amino acid; its configuration is R only because of how its groups rank.

choices.text: Its side chain ranks lower than the hydrogen on the α carbon
choices.why: Any carbon substituent outranks hydrogen; the point is that –CH2SH outranks –CO2H.

explanation: In other L amino acids the –CO2H group ranks above the side chain, giving S. In cysteine, sulfur (higher atomic number than oxygen) on the side-chain carbon makes –CH2SH rank higher than –CO2H, so the same spatial arrangement is labeled R (Exercise 26.1.2).

prompt: Threonine is (2S,3R)-2-amino-3-hydroxybutanoic acid. Which stereoisomer is its enantiomer?

choices.why: Only one chirality center is changed, so this is a diastereomer of threonine.
Only one chirality center is changed, so this is a diastereomer of threonine.
This is threonine itself, not its enantiomer.

explanation: Threonine has two chirality centers (Exercise 26.1.3). Its enantiomer has both centers inverted, (2R,3S). Inverting just one center, as in (2S,3S) or (2R,3R), gives a diastereomer.

prompt: How many of the 20 common amino acids in Table 26.1.1 contain aromatic rings?
explanation: Exercise 26.1.1: four amino acids contain aromatic rings: phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, and histidine.

prompt: Which two of the 20 common amino acids contain sulfur?

choices.why: Serine's side chain is an alcohol, –CH2OH, with no sulfur.
Threonine has an alcohol side chain, not a sulfur group.
Tyrosine has a phenol side chain; it contains no sulfur.

explanation: Exercise 26.1.1: the sulfur-containing amino acids are cysteine (a thiol, –CH2SH) and methionine (–CH2CH2SCH3).

prompt: According to the answer to Exercise 26.1.1, how many of the 20 common amino acids have hydrocarbon side chains?
explanation: The amino acids with hydrocarbon side chains are alanine, isoleucine, leucine, valine, and phenylalanine: five in all. By comparison, Ser and Thr have alcohol side chains and Cys and Met contain sulfur.

prompt: How many of the 20 protein amino acids are essential amino acids that humans must obtain in the diet?
explanation: Humans can biosynthesize only 11 of the 20 protein amino acids, the nonessential amino acids. The other 9, the essential amino acids, are biosynthesized only in plants and microorganisms and must come from the diet.

prompt: Why is tyrosine sometimes considered a nonessential amino acid?

choices.text: Humans can make it from phenylalanine, an essential amino acid
Humans can produce it from tryptophan, which is nonessential
choices.why: The book says tyrosine is made from phenylalanine, and phenylalanine is essential.

choices.text: It is not one of the 20 amino acids found in proteins
choices.why: Tyrosine is one of the 20 common amino acids in proteins (Table 26.1.1).

choices.text: Most of it comes from the diet, as with arginine
choices.why: That describes arginine. Tyrosine counts as nonessential because the body can make it from phenylalanine.

explanation: The essential/nonessential division isn't clear-cut. Tyrosine is sometimes considered nonessential because humans can produce it from phenylalanine, but phenylalanine itself is essential. Arginine can be synthesized by humans, but much of what we need comes from the diet.
